blocks.content: **{{term:funktionsanalyse|Function analysis}}** is the usual first step of a {{term:triz|TRIZ}} problem analysis. It breaks a technical system down into components, records which components {{term:wechselwirkung|interact}}, and describes every interaction as a function: **carrier – verb – object**.

items: **Components** — one target (what the main function acts on), the system components and the elements of the {{term:supersystem|supersystem}}.

**Interactions** — tick the pairs in the matrix that touch or influence each other. Every tick is a candidate for at least one function. A second click sets an “x”: the pair is deliberately excluded; a third click clears the cell.

**Function model** — every pair has a block of its own; clicking an open pair creates it with its first arrow. + adds another arrow on the pair (e.g. for the opposite direction), the arrow button reverses the direction. Every function is useful (adequate, insufficient, excessive) or harmful. The rank follows from the object: acting on the target = basic function, on the supersystem = additional function, on a system component = auxiliary function. Auxiliary functions are graded by their distance: A₁ acts on a component that carries a basic or additional function itself, A₂ on one that carries an A₁ function, and so on; the shortest way counts. Without a way to a basic or additional function it reads just “A”. **Show function ranks** writes the codes B, Ad and A₁…Aₙ on the arrows, also in the export.

blocks.content: Harmful, insufficient and excessive functions appear in the **disadvantage list**. They are the starting point for {{term:substanz-feld-analyse|Su-Field analysis}} and the contradiction tools.

Components can be dragged, and so can the verbs on the arrows: the arrow then bends at the verb. The layout is saved. "Reset layout" restores the automatic start layout and straightens all arrows. Clicking a component or a function highlights it and the related arrows.

In the **Components** tab every system component gets a field for its cost in euros. The target and the supersystem are not part of the system and have no cost. A component’s **function value** is not entered but computed from the function model: every useful function it carries counts by its rank — basic function 3, additional function 2, auxiliary function 1. Harmful functions and incomplete drafts count 0.

items: **Normalisation** — value and cost are scaled to 0 to 10: the component with the highest value or cost gets 10, the others proportionally.
**Plot** — x = normalised function value, y = normalised cost. Components without a cost are left out of the plot and show “–” in the table.
**Quadrants** — the dashed lines at 5 split the plot. The top left holds components with little function and high cost: they are the first candidates for **trimming**.

blocks.content: The target is the **plaque**. The bristles remove it (useful but **insufficient** — the gaps are hardly reached), the toothpaste dissolves it. Brush head, handle and hand hold or guide — auxiliary and additional functions. The hand presses the handle too hard (**excessive**); then the bristles **injure** the gums, and the plaque itself **irritates** them (both harmful). The disadvantage list names exactly these four points. Every pair in the matrix is decided: a tick for pairs that interact, an “x” for all others. Under **Value & cost** every system component has its manufacturing cost per piece: bristles €0.06, brush head €0.04, handle €0.15. The handle carries only an auxiliary function but costs the most — it sits top left and is the first candidate for trimming. The example can be loaded from the example projects.
